subject: rockets
title: How a Rocket Pushes Off
summary: A rocket shoots hot gas down, and the gas pushes the rocket up. It even works in space.

keys.prompt: How does a rocket move forward?
keys.answer: It pushes hot gas out its back. The gas pushes the rocket forward.

options.text: It pushes gas out the back, and the gas pushes it forward
It pushes on the air in front of it
Gravity pulls it up into the sky

keys.prompt: Why can a rocket work in space, where there is no air?
keys.answer: A rocket carries everything it needs. It does not need air like a jet does.

options.text: It carries everything it needs, so it does not need air
Space is full of air for it to use
It turns its engine off in space and floats up

keys.prompt: What has to be true for a rocket to lift off?
keys.answer: Its push up, called thrust, must be bigger than gravity's pull down.

options.text: Its push up must be bigger than gravity's pull down
It must be lighter than a feather
It must wait for a windy day

cards.title: Throw and roll
cards.text: Imagine you stand on a skateboard. You hold a heavy ball. You throw it forward as hard as you can. What happens to you?

cards.question: How fast does a rocket need to go to stay up in orbit around Earth?

options.text: About 180 miles per hour
About 1,800 miles per hour
At least 17,800 miles per hour

cards.reveal: At least 17,800 miles per hour! NASA says a rocket must go that fast, above most of the air, to stay in orbit.

cards.title: Push back, go forward
cards.text: A rocket burns fuel and makes hot gas. It pushes the gas out its back. The gas pushes the rocket forward. This is Newton's third law: every action has an equal and opposite reaction.
cards.example: On the skateboard, you push the ball forward. The ball pushes you back, so you roll the other way.

why.q: Why does the ball go farther than you do?
why.a: You are heavier than the ball. NASA says that is why the ball moves farther than the person.

examples_by_interest.soccer: Say… you stand on a skateboard and do a hard soccer throw-in. You roll back a little. The ball is light, so it zooms away.

cards.title: No air needed
cards.text: A jet engine needs air to work. A rocket engine does not. It carries with it everything it needs. That is why a rocket works in space, where there is no air.
cards.example: Some rockets burn liquid fuel. Others burn solid fuel. Fireworks and model rockets use solid fuel.

why.q: Why can't a jet plane fly to space?
why.a: A jet needs air to work. Space has no air, so a jet engine can't run there.

cards.title: Beat gravity
cards.text: Earth's gravity pulls down on a rocket. The push from the hot gas is called thrust. To lift off, the thrust pushing up must be bigger than gravity pulling down.
cards.example: That is why the biggest, heaviest spacecraft need the biggest rockets and the most fuel.

cards.title: Super fast to stay up
cards.text: To stay in orbit, a rocket must reach at least 17,800 miles per hour. It must also fly above most of the air. Then it can let its satellite go.
cards.example: The space station circles about 250 miles up. It moves about 17,150 miles per hour. That is almost 5 miles every second!

cards.question: What else around you moves by pushing something the other way?
nudges: Think about swimming, rowing a boat, or walking.
What do your hands or feet push on? Which way do you go?

questions.q: A rocket pushes hot gas out its back. What happens next?

options.text: The gas pushes the rocket forward
options.why: Yes. Action and reaction go in opposite ways.

options.text: The rocket stops moving
options.why: The push on the gas gives the rocket a push too.

options.text: The gas pulls the rocket backward
options.why: The rocket goes the opposite way from the gas.

questions.q: Why can a rocket work in space?

options.text: It carries everything it needs
options.why: Right. It does not need air.

options.text: Space is full of air
options.why: Space has no air. That is why jets can't go there.

options.text: It is pulled by the Moon
options.why: The rocket moves by pushing out its own gas.

questions.q: To lift off the ground, a rocket's thrust must be…

options.text: Bigger than gravity's pull
options.why: Yes. The push up has to win.

options.text: Smaller than gravity's pull
options.why: Then the rocket would stay on the pad.

options.text: Exactly zero
options.why: With no thrust, nothing pushes the rocket up.

sources.title: What Is a Rocket? (Grades K-4)
sources.supports: Rocket engines turn fuel into hot gas and push it out the back, which moves the rocket forward; a jet engine needs air but a rocket carries everything it needs and works in space; liquid and solid fuels, fireworks and model rockets use solid fuel; Newton's third law (equal and opposite reaction); skateboard and bowling ball example, heavier person so the ball moves farther.

sources.title: How Do We Launch Things Into Space?
sources.supports: Exhaust pushes down (action) and the rocket moves up (reaction); gravity pulls down; thrust must be greater than gravity to launch; heaviest spacecraft need the biggest rockets and most propellant; at least 17,800 mph and above most of the atmosphere to stay in orbit; rocket releases the satellite; ISS about 250 miles up at about 17,150 mph.
